newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Red Cross rescues orphans in Congo truce.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross rescues orphans in Congo truce.

text.p: The Red Cross rescued 60 orphans on Friday from a no-man's land in the heart of Congo's war-ravaged capital Brazzaville, where officials said hopes were high of extending a truce that ends at midnight.
France has pulled out most of its 1,250 soldiers sent to evacuate foreign nationals, despite a U.N. plea for them to stay, but Paris kept open a possible future mediation role.

An international Red Cross (ICRC) team picked up the children who had been cared for by two nuns at an orphanage near the airport that was the city's prime target during 12 days of fighting that erupted on June 5.

"The operation went smoothly and they were taken to a Red Cross centre in Bacongo suburb. They will stay there for now," ICRC spokesman Nic Sommer said in the twin city of Kinshasa, across the Congo river in former Zaire.

The southern suburb, controlled by a neutral leader who has tried to mediate in the conflict between President Pascal Lissouba and his rival, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, has been a refuge for thousands of civilians.
Residents said Brazzaville, torn apart by the unexpected factional warfare that flared ahead of now doomed presidential elections, was peaceful on Friday.

Some ventured out for the first time in two weeks into streets still strewn with decomposing corpses, mostly of civilians caught in crossfire. The Red Cross said it plannned to start burying them as soon as possible.
The presidency said it hoped fresh talks between the two sides would lead to a formal extension of the ceasefire, which they have already agreed to try to hold "as long as possible".
"The talks have restarted now and we are all optimistic. No one wants war," Lissouba's protocol chief Maurice Mavoungou said by telephone.

African mediators in neighbouring Gabon called on Thursday for the U.N. Security Council to support deployment of an African force to help restore peace to Brazzaville. The clashes have not spread elsewhere in the oil-producing country.
U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, in a Friday interview on French radio, again asked France to stay on until such a force arrives in order to prevent a dangerous power vacuum.
French officials said only 200-300 soldiers remained in Brazzaville and would be out by Sunday.
But Paris kept its options open for a possible future role.
"We are ready to make a contribution to making this mediation work, but I cannot yet be specific," a foreign ministry spokesman told Radio France Internationale.
He said Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine would fly to New York for talks on the Congo on Monday with U.N. Secretary- General Kofi Annan.

After losing face in Africa by backing Zaire's president Mobutu Sese Seko, ousted last month by rebel leader Laurent Kabila, Paris has taken a less confident line in dealings with its former colonies, analysts say.
Congo's trouble began when Lissouba tried to disarm the militia of Sassou Nguesso, whom he had succeeded as president in 1992.
